1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: Basic information: A 29-year-old male patient was admitted to the Department of Cardiology of our hospital on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "recurrent chest tightness and palpitations for 2 months." This young male patient had recurrent palpitations and chest tightness for 2 months without an obvious precipitating cause, with a subjective marked increase in heart rate; each episode lasted from several minutes to half an hour, and the palpitations could gradually terminate after rest. During episodes, there was no headache, blackout, or syncope. On Day -14, the patient's palpitations recurred, and he then presented to a local hospital, where the following were completed: CBC: white blood cell count 13.36x109/L, hemoglobin 213 g/L; blood biochemistry: ALT 71.2 U/L, uric acid 428 umol/L, potassium 5.91 mmol/L; 12-lead ECG suggested wide QRS tachycardia, and sinus rhythm was restored after ventricular rate control (specific medication unknown). For further diagnosis and treatment, he presented to the Department of Cardiology of our hospital and was admitted from the outpatient clinic with a diagnosis of "wide QRS tachycardia." The patient was unmarried and usually healthy; he denied underlying cardiopulmonary disease and denied a family history of hereditary disease; he had a history of snoring during sleep; 3 years ago, he underwent "cholecystectomy" at a local hospital. His parents are healthy. He had two older sisters who are deceased (the eldest sister died of illness at age 5 [died 1 hour after onset following abdominal pain; details unclear]; the second sister died of illness at age 17 [died 1 week after onset; specific illness unknown]). Physical examination: T: 36.5℃, R: 20 breaths/min, P: 80 beats/min, BP: 128/74 mmHg, height: 165 cm, weight: 82 kg, MBI: 30.1 kg/m2, SpO2 on room air: 71%. He was alert and in fair general condition. Cyanosis of the lips was present. No mandibular retrognathia, macroglossia, posterior displacement of the tongue base, low-lying soft palate, no uvular hypertrophy, no tonsillar enlargement, and a slightly narrowed pharyngeal cavity. Breath sounds were clear in both lungs, with no dry or moist rales. Cardiac borders were not enlarged, rhythm was regular, and heart sounds were normal. The abdomen was distended, without tenderness or rebound tenderness. No edema of either lower extremity. No digital clubbing. Admission ancillary examinations: Arterial blood gas on Day 0: pH 7.35, PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 56 mmHg, HCO3- 30.9 mmol/L, BE 3.2 mmol/L, FiO2 29%. CBC: RBC 6.19x1012/L, HGB 193 g/L, white blood cell count normal. Blood biochemistry: AST 45 U/L, ALT 60 U/L, CHOL 6.15 mmol/L, TG 4.51 mmol/L, CK 357 U/L, lactate 3.12 mmol/L; fasting blood glucose, renal function, electrolytes, and troponin were normal. DIC screen: no abnormality detected. Thyroid function: no abnormality detected. Preoperative eight-item panel: no abnormality detected. Urinalysis: urine protein +-. 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, ST-T changes, poor R-wave progression in the anterior wall leads. Holter monitoring: average heart rate 77 beats/min, minimum heart rate 47 beats/min, maximum heart rate 112 beats/min, no pause greater than 2.0 seconds. Conclusion: 1. Sinus rhythm, paroxysmal sinus bradycardia, intermittent intraventricular conduction block with ST-T changes; 2. Abnormal Q waves and ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, and V3; 3. HRV normal. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring: normal. Brain MRI: small amount of white matter hyperintensity in the bilateral frontal and parietal lobes (Fazekas grade 1); bilateral sphenoid sinusitis, right frontal sinusitis, and right maxillary sinusitis. Cardiac MRI: 1. Mild cardiomegaly; no other definite abnormality on cardiac MRI. 2. Trace mitral regurgitation and tricuspid regurgitation. 3. Mild widening of the main pulmonary artery. Cardiac dual-source CT: 1. Myocardial bridge in the mid left anterior descending coronary artery, approximately 59.1 in length, without obvious luminal stenosis. 2. No definite atherosclerotic plaque identified in either coronary artery. Pulmonary CTA: increased bronchovascular markings in both lungs. A few linear opacities were seen in the medial segment of the right middle lobe and the inferior lingular segment of the left upper lobe. Heterogeneous thymic density in the anterior superior mediastinum, considered incomplete thymic involution. Enlarged cardiac silhouette. No abnormality in morphology or course of the main pulmonary artery, right and left main pulmonary arteries, or the lobar, segmental, and subsegmental pulmonary arteries; luminal opacification was good, and no definite filling defect lesion was seen. Vascular ultrasound of both lower extremities: no abnormality detected. Echocardiography: mild tricuspid regurgitation. No abnormality of left ventricular systolic or diastolic function. Estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure approximately 37 mmHg. EF: 68%. Pulmonary function: moderate to severe restrictive ventilatory dysfunction. Decreased total lung capacity, normal residual volume, increased RV/TLC%. Increased total respiratory impedance, increased total airway resistance, increased central airway resistance, normal peripheral elastic resistance. Normal diffusing capacity.

images.near_text: At the request of Cardiology, a consultation was performed by the Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine, with the following recommendations:

differential_diagnoses.name: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome with obstructive sleep apnea
supporting_evidence: Weight 82 kg, height 165 cm, BMI 30.1 kg/m2
History of snoring during sleep

Physical examination showed cyanosis of the lips, macroglossia, posterior displacement of the tongue base, a low-hanging soft palate, and slight narrowing of the pharyngeal cavity, suggesting the presence of anatomic upper airway narrowing factors.
Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaCO2 56 mmHg and HCO3- 30.9 mmol/L, suggesting chronic hypercapnia with compensation
SpO2 71% without supplemental oxygen, PaO2 70 mmHg, hypoxemia present
CBC: RBC 6.19x10^12/L, HGB 193g/L; previous HGB 213g/L, consistent with secondary erythrocytosis due to chronic hypoxia
PFT showed moderate-to-severe restrictive ventilatory dysfunction, decreased total lung capacity, consistent with possible obesity/chest wall load-related hypoventilation.

Pulmonary CTA and the accompanying first-phase chest CT images showed no obvious extensive consolidation, diffuse interstitial lung disease, or definite evidence of pulmonary embolism, which is difficult to explain such marked hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and more strongly supports a hypoventilation mechanism.
opposing_evidence: Age 29 years, relatively young
PFT indicated concomitant increased total respiratory impedance and increased total airway resistance, suggesting that more than simple obesity hypoventilation alone may be involved as a mechanism.
The phase 1 information did not provide sleep monitoring results, so it cannot yet be directly confirmed.

differential_diagnoses.name: Primary arrhythmia syndrome (Brugada syndrome or other channelopathies)
supporting_evidence: Young male, recurrent palpitations and chest tightness for 2 months; a prior 12-lead electrocardiogram indicated wide QRS tachycardia.
Holter ECG showed abnormal Q waves and ST-segment elevation in leads V1, V2, and V3
12-lead ECG showed ST-T changes and poor R-wave progression in the anterior leads

No clear evidence of structural heart disease: echocardiography showed no abnormalities in left ventricular systolic or diastolic function, EF 68%; dual-source CT showed no obvious coronary atherosclerosis; cardiac MRI showed no definite abnormalities except for slight cardiac enlargement.
There is a suspicious family history suggestive of sudden death: two elder sisters died of unknown causes in childhood/young adulthood.
opposing_evidence: The first-stage information did not provide a description of a typical Brugada-type electrocardiogram, only indicating ST-segment elevation in the right precordial leads, which lacks specificity.
No blackout or syncope during episodes
Ambulatory ECG did not record sustained ventricular arrhythmia

differential_diagnoses.name: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy or other genetic cardiomyopathies
supporting_evidence: Young male with wide QRS tachycardia, suggesting possible ventricular arrhythmia.
Holter ECG showed abnormal Q waves and ST-segment elevation in V1-V3, suggesting abnormalities in the right precordial leads
Cardiac MRI showed slight enlargement of the heart and mild widening of the main pulmonary artery; enlarged cardiac silhouette
There is a family history of unexplained death at a young age, suggesting possible hereditary heart disease.
opposing_evidence: Cardiac MRI indicated, "No definite abnormality was seen in the remainder of the cardiac MRI"; there was no definite description of right ventricular structural abnormality or fibrofatty infiltration abnormality.
Color Doppler echocardiography showed normal left ventricular function, with no definite evidence of cardiomyopathy
The information from the first stage did not provide typical ARVC-related ECG details such as epsilon waves.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary hypertension (possibly related to sleep-disordered breathing/hypoventilation; idiopathic or other types also need to be differentiated)
supporting_evidence: SpO2 71% without supplemental oxygen, with marked hypoxemia, which may cause or exacerbate increased pulmonary circulatory pressure
Echocardiography estimated the pulmonary artery systolic pressure at approximately 37 mmHg, suggesting mildly elevated pulmonary artery pressure
Cardiac MRI showed mild enlargement of the main pulmonary artery
Manifestations of chronic hypoxemia include cyanosis of the lips and polycythemia.
The patient has chest tightness and palpitations.
opposing_evidence: Pulmonary artery pressure was only mildly elevated, which is still insufficient to independently explain the severe hypoxemia
Pulmonary CTA showed good opacification of the main pulmonary artery, the left and right pulmonary arteries, and branches at all levels, with no definite filling defects.
Echocardiography did not indicate obvious right heart dysfunction or severe tricuspid regurgitation.

differential_diagnoses.name: Right-to-left shunt disorders (occult shunt in cyanotic congenital heart disease/patent foramen ovale-related shunt/intrapulmonary shunt)
supporting_evidence: At rest, SpO2 was only 71%, with lip cyanosis and marked erythrocytosis, suggesting chronic hypoxemia.
Lung auscultation was clear; pulmonary CTA and the accompanying first-stage chest CT images showed no obvious pulmonary parenchymal lesions sufficient to explain the severe hypoxemia
Cardiac MRI showed only slight cardiac enlargement and mild widening of the main pulmonary artery; an occult shunt cannot be completely excluded.
In a young patient with marked hypoxemia and only mild abnormalities on routine lung imaging, intracardiac or intrapulmonary shunt should be considered.
opposing_evidence: Echocardiography did not report definite congenital structural abnormalities.
No clubbing of the fingers or toes
Pulmonary CTA did not indicate a definite pulmonary arteriovenous malformation or major vascular abnormality.
Stage I information did not provide evidence from contrast echocardiography or transesophageal echocardiography

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary embolism/chronic thromboembolic pulmonary vascular disease
supporting_evidence: The patient has hypoxemia, chest tightness, and palpitations, which can be seen in pulmonary vascular thromboembolic disease.

Cardiac MRI showed mild widening of the main pulmonary artery, and echocardiography estimated the pulmonary artery systolic pressure at approximately 37 mmHg, which may be consistent with increased pulmonary vascular load
opposing_evidence: Pulmonary CTA clearly showed no abnormalities in the morphology or course of the main pulmonary artery, the right and left main pulmonary arteries, or the lobar, segmental, and subsegmental pulmonary arteries; luminal opacification was good, and no definite filling defect was seen.
No abnormalities were found on vascular ultrasound of both lower extremities
Symptoms recurred over 2 months, without clear acute chest pain, hemoptysis, or manifestations of lower extremity deep vein thrombosis in the initial stage
The attached first-stage chest CT images did not show typical imaging findings of pulmonary infarction

recommended_exams.exam: Complete the relevant examinations and actively investigate the cause of restrictive ventilatory dysfunction.
Request a Sleep Medicine consultation, complete sleep monitoring, and use a ventilator if necessary (perform pressure titration to determine the appropriate settings).

stage2_input.text: After consultation with the Sleep Medicine Department, polysomnography was recommended. On Day +2, portable polysomnography showed: AHI 36.5 events/hour, OSA 34 episodes, CSA 23 episodes, MSA 10 episodes, HP 182 episodes, longest apnea duration: 48 seconds, longest hypopnea duration: 79 seconds, mean oxygen saturation 82%, lowest oxygen saturation 40%, and oxygen saturation below 90% accounted for 90% of the total monitoring time. Among these, the decrease in oxygen saturation was more pronounced during REM sleep, significantly lower than during NREM sleep. On Day +5, the patient was instructed to go to the Sleep Medicine Department for overnight attended pressure titration. The PSG monitoring report during pressure titration showed: AHI 14.5 events/hour, OSA 2 episodes, CSA 24 episodes, MSA 0 episodes, HP 43 episodes, longest apnea duration: 17 seconds, longest hypopnea duration: 33.5 seconds, mean oxygen saturation 87%, lowest oxygen saturation 61%. Arterial blood gas analysis before pressure titration showed: pH 7.37, PaO2 45 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3- 29.5 mmol/L, BE 2.7 mmol/L, FiO2: 21%; morning arterial blood gas analysis after pressure titration showed: pH 7.40, PaO2 58 mmHg, PaCO2 46 mmHg, HCO3- 28.7 mmol/L, BE 3.0 mmol/L, FiO2: 29%. On Day +7, the patient was transferred to the Sleep Medicine Department for further diagnosis and treatment. Repeat polysomnography and simultaneous transcutaneous carbon dioxide monitoring further confirmed that the patient had sleep-related alveolar hypoventilation. Noninvasive ventilatory support treatment was continued in the Sleep Medicine Department. Overnight oxygen saturation monitoring showed a mean oxygen saturation of 92%, lowest oxygen saturation 75%, and 4% oxygen desaturation index (ODI4) 7.8 events/hour. Repeat arterial blood gas analysis after ventilator treatment showed: pH 7.38, PaO2 65 mmHg, PaCO2 52 mmHg, HCO3- 27.3 mmol/L, BE 0.4 mmol/L, FiO2: 33%. Further evaluation of respiratory center regulatory function was completed, and repeat ECG and Holter monitoring were performed: the respiratory center drive function test results showed: 1. hypoxic respiratory center drive responsiveness was 0.17 L.min-1.%-1, lower than the laboratory normal value; 2. hypercapnic respiratory center drive responsiveness was 0.51 L.min-1.mmHg-1, lower than the laboratory normal value. Repeat ECG showed: sinus rhythm; ST-T changes (elevation); clockwise rotation of the heart; first-degree atrioventricular block. Repeat Holter monitoring showed: average heart rate 70 beats/min, slowest heart rate 42 beats/min, fastest heart rate 141 beats/min, no pause greater than 2.0 seconds. There were 187 premature ventricular contractions, with the highest number occurring at 11 o'clock at 60; there was 1 run of ventricular bigeminy and 11 runs of ventricular trigeminy. The conclusions were as follows: 1. sinus rhythm, paroxysmal prolonged R-R interval (maximum 1.82 seconds); 2. occasional premature ventricular contractions, paroxysmal bigeminy and trigeminy; 3. intraventricular conduction block; 4. poor R-wave progression in leads V1-V3, ST-T changes in some leads, and paroxysmal abnormal Q waves in leads I and AVL; 5. HRV normal. Further electromyography/evoked potential testing in the Department of Neurology was completed. Neurology consultation physical examination: since junior high school, the patient had poor athletic performance; limb weakness could occur at the beginning of activity, and symptoms could improve after repeated activity; there was no obvious limb fatigue, and the patient felt it did not affect daily life. Denied myoedema after percussion. Short and stocky body habitus, cyanotic lips, slight baldness, bilateral eyelids covering the pupils, ptotic and everted, mouth breathing, well-developed and tight limb muscles, mild bilateral cataracts, ocular movements intact in all directions, pupils briskly reactive to light, eyelid closure strength preserved, instantaneous muscle strength of all four limbs grade 5, brisk tendon reflexes, no pathologic reflexes elicited, and obvious myotonia could be elicited.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: According to the Neurology consultation recommendations, muscle biopsy and genetic testing were completed. The results of the muscle biopsy and genetic testing were as follows:
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 29-year-old man. In addition to recurrent chest tightness, palpitations, and wide-QRS tachycardia, more importantly there are clues of long-standing progressive neuromuscular involvement: since junior high school, he has had poor athletic performance, with limb weakness at the beginning of activity that improves after repeated activity; physical examination showed a short, stocky body habitus, mild balding, bilateral ptosis with ectropion, mouth breathing, well-developed and tense muscles of the extremities, mild bilateral cataracts, and marked myotonia could be elicited. At the same time, the patient has moderate-to-severe restrictive ventilatory dysfunction, chronic hypercapnia, severe sleep-related hypoxemia, and sleep-related alveolar hypoventilation, and neither the pulmonary imaging findings nor the cardiac structural abnormalities are sufficient to fully explain his type II respiratory failure, suggesting that a neuromuscular disease as the more central etiology should be investigated. Muscle biopsy can directly assess whether a myopathic lesion is present and its pathologic features, helping differentiate among myotonic dystrophy, other muscular dystrophies, metabolic myopathy, inflammatory myopathy, and other differential diagnoses; it can also be combined with the prior mild CK elevation and subsequent clues from EMG/evoked potentials to confirm respiratory muscle involvement and the nature of the systemic myopathy. Clarifying the pathologic type is critical for explaining whether his hypoventilation, restrictive ventilatory dysfunction, arrhythmia, and ocular manifestations belong to the same systemic disease, for determining prognosis, and for guiding subsequent genetic counseling, respiratory support, and cardiac monitoring strategies.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: According to the Neurology consultation recommendations, muscle biopsy and genetic testing were completed. The results of the muscle biopsy and genetic testing were as follows:
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: This case is clinically highly suggestive of a hereditary neuromuscular disease, especially the myotonic dystrophy spectrum: the patient has obvious myotonia, poor exercise tolerance with onset in adolescence, ptosis and ectropion, mild cataracts, a balding appearance, mouth breathing, and restrictive ventilatory impairment, and has developed sleep-related alveolar hypoventilation, chronic hypercapnia, and arrhythmias/conduction abnormalities; these manifestations indicate multisystem involvement. The patient also has two older sisters who died of unknown causes in childhood or young adulthood. Although the family history is incomplete, it still suggests a potential genetic background. The core purpose of genetic testing is molecular confirmation of suspected hereditary myopathy, particularly to determine whether there are pathogenic variants related to myotonic dystrophy type 1, thereby unifying the disparate respiratory, cardiac, ocular, and skeletal muscle manifestations under the same etiologic framework. This test not only helps establish the final diagnosis and exclude other hereditary myopathies with similar phenotypes, but will also directly affect subsequent management, including arrhythmia risk stratification and follow-up, the long-term plan for ventilator therapy, family screening and genetic counseling, and prediction of disease progression and complications. Therefore, in the context of a neurology consultation that has already clearly raised suspicion for myotonic myopathy, genetic testing is the key confirmatory test.

8.final_diagnosis_and_diagnostic_basis.final_diagnosis: 1. Secondary sleep-related alveolar hypoventilation due to neuromuscular disease 2. Type II respiratory failure 3. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) 4. Arrhythmia 5. Bilateral cataracts (early stage) 6. Secondary erythrocytosis 7. Pulmonary hypertension 8. Liver injury 9. Hyperlipidemia 10. Hyperuricemia 11. Myocardial bridge

treatment_plan: The ventilator treatment settings were gradually adjusted to: oronasal mask, lateral position, head of bed elevated 30°, BiPAP-S/T (EPAP 9 cmH2O, IPAP 24 cmH2O), backup respiratory rate 15 breaths/min, supplemental oxygen 1 L/min
After discharge, continue ventilator therapy with the same settings, without supplemental oxygen
Antiarrhythmic treatment: bisoprolol 2.5-5 mg qd, adjust the dose according to heart rate
treatment_response: Overnight pulse oximetry monitoring: average oxygen saturation 93%, lowest oxygen saturation 86%, ODI 45.6 events/hour
Repeat morning arterial blood gas analysis after treatment: pH 7.41, PaO2 70 mmHg, PaCO2 41 mmHg, HCO3- 25.2 mmol/L, BE 1.4 mmol/L
Mechanical ventilation was effective, and type II respiratory failure was corrected
At the 3-month telephone follow-up, the patient continued nocturnal ventilator therapy and had no further palpitations or chest tightness.
